mainTopic: The עבד עברי who ran away or got sick, and the amount and type of his הענקה (parting gift)
overview: This amud starts by finishing a ברייתא about an עבד עברי: a slave who got sick still goes free in the seventh year. רב ששת explains that a runaway slave set free by the יובל still loses his הענקה (parting gift). The גמרא then compares two ברייתות on sick slaves. One who can still do light work like sewing never makes up time, but one who could not work for four or more years must make up the time. Next a ברייתא gives three opinions on the size of the הענקה: רבי מאיר says fifteen סלעים, רבי יהודה says thirty, and רבי שמעון says fifty. The גמרא traces each amount to a גזירה שוה: ריקם from בכור, נתינה from the gored slave, and נתינה from ערכין. It also defends each choice against the other sources. Then it shows that the words צאן, גורן, יקב teach what kind of thing may be given: something 'blessed' that grows. רבי שמעון leaves out money and רבי אליעזר בן יעקב leaves out mules. The amud ends by asking why 'winepress' is needed, and the answer comes on the next amud.

steps.title: A sick slave still goes free in the seventh year
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא ends by teaching that a slave who got sick does not have to add extra years. The פסוק says he goes out in the seventh year no matter what.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might think that even a slave who got sick must make up the lost time. So the פסוק says: 'And in the seventh he shall go out.'
steps.whatsHappening: This is the last line of a ברייתא that began on the previous daf. It teaches that a slave who was sick does not need to make up his missed years.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא compared the sick slave to the runaway, who does have to make up his time. Here it says the sick slave is different. The words 'in the seventh he shall go out' show that he leaves on time even though he could not work.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have thought (opens a wrong assumption)
The verse teaches (brings the פסוק that rules out the wrong idea)
And in the seventh year he shall go out

phrases.english: One might think: even if he became sick [he must make up the time]?
The verse teaches: "And in the seventh he shall go out."
phrases.notes: שמות 21:2

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the ברייתא quoted on the previous daf.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A slave who was sick during his term does not make up the lost time. He goes out in the seventh year.

steps.title: The runaway case is one where the יובל freed him
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת explains that the ברייתא's runaway case is about a slave who fled and was then freed by the יובל. Even so, he loses his הענקה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת said: Here we are dealing with a slave who ran away, and then the יובל came. You might have said that since the יובל freed him, he counts as 'sent away from you,' so we should not penalize him and should give him the gift. The ברייתא teaches us that he still does not get it.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת explains what case the ברייתא meant when it said a runaway slave gets no הענקה. He says it is a slave who ran away and was freed by the יובל before finishing his years.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A normal runaway has to make up his time anyway, so he would get the gift at the end. That is why the ברייתא's rule needed explaining. רב ששת's case is one where the slave never makes up the time, because the יובל frees him. You might think the יובל's release makes him 'sent away' and earns him the gift. The ברייתא teaches that running away cost him the gift anyway.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here?
The Jubilee (50th) year, when all Hebrew slaves go free
You might have said (introduces the mistaken idea)
The parting gift a master must give a freed עבד עברי

steps.confusionAlert: רב ששת is not explaining the sick-slave line just above. He is going back to the runaway part of the ברייתא from the previous daf.

phrases.english: Rav Sheshet said:
With what are we dealing here?
phrases.notes: He is talking about the runaway slave in the ברייתא, who loses his gift.

phrases.english: For example, where he ran away and the Jubilee year came upon him.
You might have said:
Since the Jubilee released him,
we call him "sent away from you,"
phrases.notes: These words come from דברים 15:13, the verse that commands the gift when you send a slave free.

phrases.english: so we should not penalize him, and we should give him the gift,
it teaches us [that he does not get it].

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב שֵׁשֶׁת: הָכָא בְּמַאי עָסְקִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the runaway part of the same ברייתא and explains the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the יובל released him, he counts as 'sent away' and should get the הענקה.
steps.terutzMaskana: A slave who ran away loses his הענקה even if the יובל later freed him.

steps.title: Quoting the sick-slave line again
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the ברייתא's sick-slave rule again, so it can question it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: You might think that even a slave who got sick must make up the time. So the פסוק says: 'And in the seventh he shall go out.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back and quotes the sick-slave line again. This is a setup: the גמרא is about to challenge it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing new is ruled here. The words are repeated so the reader knows which line the next question is aimed at.

phrases.english: The Master said:
One might think: even if he became sick [he must make up the time];
the verse teaches: "And in the seventh he shall go out."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the runaway topic and goes back to the sick-slave line to examine it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Restates that a sick slave goes out in the seventh year without making up time.

steps.title: Another ברייתא says a slave sick all six years must make up the time
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: does this hold even if he was sick all six years? Another ברייתא says three sick years need no make-up, but six sick years do.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even if he was sick all six years? But a ברייתא teaches: If he was sick three years and worked three, he does not have to complete. If he was sick all six, he does have to complete!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the sick-slave rule with a different ברייתא. That ברייתא says a slave who was sick the whole six years must make up the time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first ברייתא sounds like sickness never requires make-up. The second ברייתא says it does when the sickness lasted all six years. So the two ברייתות seem to disagree.

keyTerms.meaning: To complete (make up the missing work time)

phrases.english: Even if he was sick all six [years]?
But isn't it taught [in a ברייתא]:
If he was sick three [years] and worked three,
he is not obligated to complete [the time];
if he was sick all six, he is obligated to complete!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the rule quoted in the previous step.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that a sick slave never has to make up time.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A second ברייתא says a slave sick for all six years must make up the time. This contradicts the first ברייתא, which made no such limit.

steps.title: The first ברייתא means a slave who can still do light work
steps.stepSummary: רב ששת answers that the first ברייתא is about a slave who is too sick for hard work but can still do needlework.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב ששת said: It is talking about one who can do needle work.
steps.whatsHappening: רב ששת solves the contradiction. The ברייתא that says 'no make-up' is about a sick slave who can still do light jobs like sewing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Such a slave is still giving his master some work. So he goes out on time even if he was sick all six years. The other ברייתא, which requires make-up, is about a slave who could not work at all.

phrases.english: Rav Sheshet said:
[It refers to] one who can do needlework.
phrases.notes: He means the first ברייתא, where the sick slave does not make up time.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב שֵׁשֶׁת: בְּעוֹשֶׂה מַעֲשֵׂה מַחַט
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (each ברייתא is about a different situation)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two ברייתות disagree about a slave who was sick.
steps.terutzMaskana: A sick slave who can still do light work goes out on time. One who cannot work at all, if sick long enough, must make up the time.
steps.whatToRemember: Sick but able to do light work like sewing: no make-up. Fully unable to work for the whole term: must make up the time.

steps.title: The second ברייתא seems to contradict itself about four sick years
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notices the second ברייתא contradicts itself about a slave sick for four years.
steps.simpleTranslation: This ברייתא is itself difficult. You said: sick three years and worked three, he does not have to complete. That implies that with four years sick, he must complete. Now look at the last part: sick all six years, he must complete. That implies that with four years sick, he does not have to complete!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now finds a problem inside the second ברייתא itself. Its first half and last half point in opposite directions about four years of sickness.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first half sets the limit at three: more than three sick years means make-up. The last half names six: less than six sick years means no make-up. Four years falls in between, and the two halves give opposite answers.

keyTerms.meaning: This text itself is difficult (it contradicts itself)
This implies (drawing an inference from the wording)

phrases.english: This itself is difficult:
You said: if he was sick three and worked three,
he is not obligated to complete.
This implies that with four, he is obligated to complete.
Say the last clause:
If he was sick all six, he is obligated to complete.
This implies that with four, he is not obligated to complete!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns to the ברייתא quoted in step 4 and points out an inner contradiction.
steps.kashyaTarget: The wording of the second ברייתא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Read precisely, the first half implies four sick years require make-up. The last half implies they do not.

steps.title: Four sick years count like six
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains the ברייתא's meaning: a slave sick for four years is treated like one sick all six, so he must make up the time.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what it means: if he was sick four years, he is treated like someone who was sick all six, and he must complete the time.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the contradiction by reading the last half differently. 'All six' really includes four or more years of sickness.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first half's limit is the real rule. Three sick years means no make-up, and more than three means make-up. The phrase 'all six' in the last half covers any case of four or more years, because most of the term was lost.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what it means (re-reading a text)

steps.whatToRemember: An עבד עברי who could not work at all: three sick years need no make-up. Four or more sick years count like six, and he must make up the time.

phrases.english: This is what it is saying:
If he was sick four [years],
he becomes like one who was sick all six,
and he is obligated to complete.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the inner contradiction raised in step 6.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'All six' means only a full six years of sickness.
steps.terutzMaskana: Four sick years are treated like six, so the slave must make up the time.

steps.title: Three opinions on the size of the parting gift
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא lists three amounts for the הענקה: fifteen (רבי מאיר), thirty (רבי יהודה), fifty (רבי שמעון).
steps.simpleTranslation: רבנן taught: How much do we give him as a parting gift? Five סלעים from each type, which makes fifteen. That is רבי מאיר. רבי יהודה says thirty, like the thirty of a slave. רבי שמעון says fifty, like the fifty of ערכין.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic by quoting a ברייתא about how much the master must give his freed עבד עברי as a parting gift.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each תנא ties the amount to a different amount found in the תורה. רבי יהודה uses the thirty shekels paid for a killed slave. רבי שמעון uses fifty, the highest amount in ערכין.

keyTerms.meaning: The parting gift a master must give his freed עבד עברי
Fixed valuations a person pledges to the בית המקדש

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
How much do we give him as a parting gift?
Five sela'im from each and every type,
which makes fifteen sela'im,
these are the words of Rabbi Meir.
Rabbi Yehuda says: thirty,
like the thirty of a slave.
phrases.notes: These are the thirty shekels paid when an ox kills a slave (שמות 21:32).

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon says: fifty,
like the fifty of valuations.
phrases.notes: Fifty shekels is the highest valuation amount (ויקרא 27:3).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic after the discussion of the sick slave.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר: 5 סלעים from each of 3 types (15 total). רבי יהודה: 30. רבי שמעון: 50.

steps.title: Quoting רבי מאיר's words again
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא repeats רבי מאיר's statement so it can question it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: Five סלעים from each type, which makes fifteen. These are the words of רבי מאיר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes רבי מאיר's opinion again. It is setting up the question that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The focus is the extra phrase "which makes fifteen." The next step will ask why רבי מאיר needed to say it.

phrases.english: The Master said:
Five sela'im from each and every type,
which makes fifteen sela'im,
the words of Rabbi Meir.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Re-quotes part of the ברייתא from step 8 in order to analyze it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Five סלעים per type, fifteen total.

steps.title: Why would רבי מאיר teach simple math?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבי מאיר added "which makes fifteen". Everyone knows three times five is fifteen.
steps.simpleTranslation: Did רבי מאיר come to teach us how to count?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the extra words in רבי מאיר's statement, since they seem to add nothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A תנא does not waste words. If "five from each of three" is already said, the total of fifteen looks unneeded. So the words must teach something.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Meir,
came to teach us counting?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the wording just quoted.
steps.kashyaTarget: The words "which makes fifteen סלעים" in רבי מאיר's statement
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The total is obvious arithmetic, so stating it seems to add nothing.

steps.title: The total matters, not the split
steps.stepSummary: The total of fifteen teaches that the master may not give less than fifteen. He may give less of one type and more of another.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what he teaches us: he may not give less than this total. But if he gives less of one type and more of another, we have no problem with it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that "fifteen" is there to show that the total is the real requirement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without the total, we might think each type needs exactly five. Stating fifteen shows that the minimum applies to the whole gift. The split between types can change.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what he teaches us
We have no problem with it

phrases.english: This is what he teaches us:
he must not give him less
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets; the word in square brackets is the corrected wording. Both mean "give less."

phrases.english: than this total number,
but if he gives him less of one type
and more of another type,
we have no problem with it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the purpose of the wording
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Stating fifteen seemed like needless arithmetic.
steps.terutzMaskana: Fifteen is the required minimum total. Amounts may shift between types.

steps.title: What is רבי מאיר's source?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks where רבי מאיר gets the number five.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is רבי מאיר's reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the source behind רבי מאיר's amount. It is setting up the explanation that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא gave רבי מאיר's amount without saying where it comes from. The גמרא will ask this same question about רבי יהודה (step 19) and רבי שמעון (step 25) as well.

phrases.english: What is Rabbi Meir's reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the wording of רבי מאיר's statement to its source.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The scriptural basis for five סלעים per type

steps.title: Learning "empty" from the firstborn
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר links the word ריקם in the הענקה פסוק to ריקם by a בכור, where the amount is five סלעים.
steps.simpleTranslation: He learns "empty" and "empty" from a בכור. Just as there it is five סלעים, so too here it is five סלעים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a word link. The same word "empty" appears in both places, so the same amount applies.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה says not to send the slave away ריקם. It also uses ריקם about the בכור, whose redemption is five סלעים. So the gift is five סלעים too.

keyTerms.meaning: Firstborn son, redeemed for five סלעים
Just as there... so too here: the wording of a word-link comparison

steps.confusionAlert: Five סלעים is the amount for each type, not the total. The next two steps explain why.

phrases.english: He learns "empty" "empty" from a firstborn.
phrases.notes: The two פסוקים are דברים 15:13 and שמות 34:20.

phrases.english: Just as there it is five sela'im,
so too here it is five sela'im.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 12.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A גזירה שוה of ריקם from בכור gives five סלעים.

steps.title: Maybe only five in total?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the five from the בכור should not be the total for all three types together.
steps.simpleTranslation: But say instead: five סלעים from all of them together!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges how the word link was used. The comparison only gives five, so why multiply it by three?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The בכור has one payment of five. The challenge suggests the gift should also be one five, shared across flock, grain and wine.

phrases.english: But say instead,
five sela'im from all of them together!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the conclusion drawn from the word link in step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי מאיר's ruling of five סלעים for each type
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The בכור source gives only one five, so the total should be five, not fifteen.

steps.title: "Empty" comes first, so it applies to each type
steps.stepSummary: Because ריקם is written before the list, it applies to each item on its own. So each type needs five.
steps.simpleTranslation: If "empty" were written at the end, it would be as you say. Now that "empty" is written at the beginning, apply "empty" to flock, "empty" to threshing floor, and "empty" to winepress.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers from where the word sits in the פסוקים. ריקם comes before the list, so it attaches to each item separately.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A word after a list sums up the whole list as one unit. A word before a list leads into each item one by one. So "not empty" means five for flock, five for grain and five for wine.

keyTerms.meaning: Flock, threshing floor, winepress: the three types of the gift

steps.whatToRemember: רבי מאיר: the הענקה is at least fifteen סלעים. The amount comes from ריקם by the בכור (five). Because ריקם comes before the list, each of the three types counts as five. The total is what matters, so types may be shifted.

phrases.english: If "empty" were written at the end,
it would be as you say.
Now that "empty" is written at the beginning,
phrases.notes: "Empty" ends דברים 15:13, right before the list in the next פסוק.

phrases.english: apply "empty" to "flock,"
"empty" to "threshing floor,"
"empty" to "winepress."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reading based on where the word sits in the פסוק
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The five from the בכור might be one total for all three types.
steps.terutzMaskana: ריקם comes before the list, so it applies to each type. That gives five per type, fifteen total.

steps.title: Why not learn the empty-handed rule from the festival offering?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי מאיר: ריקם also appears by עולת ראיה, which has no fixed amount, so why learn from בכור?
steps.simpleTranslation: But let us learn 'empty' and 'empty' from the burnt offering brought when coming to the בית המקדש on the festivals!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רבי מאיר's source. The word ריקם also shows up by עולת ראיה, so why not learn from there?
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר learned the number five by linking ריקם in הענקה to ריקם by בכור. But the same word appears by עולת ראיה, which has no set amount. If we learned from there, הענקה would have no fixed minimum at all.

keyTerms.meaning: And let us learn (it from somewhere else)
The burnt offering brought when a person comes to the בית המקדש on the שלש רגלים
Learning a law from one place to another because the same word appears in both

phrases.english: But let us learn 'empty' and 'empty'
phrases.notes: The פסוק there is דברים 16:16: 'they shall not appear before ה׳ empty.'

phrases.english: from the burnt offering of appearance!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the choice of בכור as the source for רבי מאיר's ריקם link.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי מאיר's גזירה שוה of ריקם from בכור
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same word ריקם appears by עולת ראיה, which has no fixed amount. So why choose בכור and its five סלעים?

steps.title: The words 'with which ה׳ blessed you' demand a real amount
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק of הענקה says 'אשר ברכך ה׳ אלהיך', which shows the gift must be a respectable amount, so it fits בכור and not עולת ראיה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: 'Of that with which ה׳ your God has blessed you.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the הענקה פסוק itself points to a generous gift. So we cannot learn from עולת ראיה, which has no set amount.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'אשר ברכך' tells us that the gift must match a blessing, meaning a real and respectable amount. That rules out learning from עולת ראיה, which has no fixed amount. The link to בכור, with its fixed five סלעים, stays in place.

phrases.english: The verse states: 'Of that with which the Lord your God has blessed you.'
phrases.notes: דברים 15:14

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A word in the פסוק blocks the other comparison
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Maybe הענקה is like עולת ראיה and has no fixed amount.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'אשר ברכך' requires a respectable amount, so we learn from בכור's five.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי מאיר's five comes from בכור. 'אשר ברכך' shows that הענקה must be a real amount, unlike עולת ראיה.

steps.title: רבי יהודה says thirty, like a slave
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings up the opinion of רבי יהודה from the ברייתא: the total gift is thirty, like the thirty paid for a slave.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: thirty, like the thirty of a slave.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now moves to the next opinion in the ברייתא. This is a setup line for the next question about רבי יהודה's source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר gave five of each type, fifteen in total. רבי יהודה gives a different total of thirty סלעים. He compares it to the thirty shekels paid for a slave.

keyTerms.meaning: The thirty shekels paid when an ox kills a slave

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:
thirty, like the thirty of a slave.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: שְׁלֹשִׁים כִּשְׁלֹשִׁים שֶׁל עֶבֶד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from רבי מאיר's view to רבי יהודה's view in the same ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי יהודה, the הענקה totals thirty סלעים.

steps.title: What is רבי יהודה's source?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבי יהודה says thirty.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason of רבי יהודה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks where רבי יהודה gets the number thirty. This sets up the explanation that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same kind of question that was asked about רבי מאיר's five in step 12. Now the same check is done for רבי יהודה.

phrases.english: What is the reasoning of Rabbi Yehuda?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the ruling in step 18.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source of רבי יהודה's number thirty.

steps.title: Learning 'giving' from the slave killed by an ox
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה links the word 'giving' in הענקה to the word 'giving' by a slave gored by an ox, where the payment is thirty.
steps.simpleTranslation: He learns 'giving' and 'giving' from a slave. Just as there it is thirty, so too here it is thirty.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that רבי יהודה uses a גזירה שוה on the word 'giving' (נתינה). By the gored slave the תורה says 'he shall give thirty shekels.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The הענקה פסוק uses the word 'give', and so does the פסוק about an ox that kills a slave. The amount there is thirty shekels, so רבי יהודה makes the הענקה total thirty as well.

keyTerms.meaning: Giving (the shared word used for the comparison)
Just as there, so too here

phrases.english: He derives 'giving' and 'giving' from a slave.
phrases.notes: The slave פסוק is שמות 21:32: 'he shall give to their master thirty shekels.'

phrases.english: Just as there it is thirty,
so too here it is thirty.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 19.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A גזירה שוה of נתינה from the thirty shekels paid for a gored slave.

steps.title: Why not learn fifty from ערכין?
steps.stepSummary: The word 'giving' also appears by ערכין, where the amount is fifty, so why not learn fifty?
steps.simpleTranslation: But let us learn 'giving' and 'giving' from ערכין: just as there it is fifty, so too here it should be fifty!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי יהודה's source. 'Giving' also appears by ערכין, so the answer could be fifty instead of thirty.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A גזירה שוה works off a shared word, and the same word נתינה also appears by ערכין. There an adult man's value is fifty shekels. So why choose the slave's thirty?

keyTerms.meaning: Pledges to give a person's set 'value' to the בית המקדש; an adult man is fifty shekels

phrases.english: But let him derive 'giving' and 'giving' from valuations;
phrases.notes: See ויקרא 27:23.

phrases.english: just as there it is fifty,
so too here it should be fifty!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the source given in step 20.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יהודה's choice of the gored slave as the source
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same word נתינה appears by ערכין, which would give fifty, so the choice of thirty seems arbitrary.

steps.title: First answer: when in doubt, take the smaller amount
steps.stepSummary: If you grab too much you may end up holding nothing, but if you grab a little you keep it. So we go with thirty.
steps.simpleTranslation: One answer: if you grasped a lot, you did not grasp; if you grasped a little, you grasped.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives its first answer. When two sources are possible, we take the smaller amount, because that much is certain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Thirty is included within fifty, so thirty is certain either way. Without clear proof we cannot force the master to give the larger amount. That is why רבי יהודה says thirty.

keyTerms.meaning: If you grab too much, you hold nothing
If you grab a little, you hold it

phrases.english: One answer: if you grasped a lot, you did not grasp;
if you grasped a little, you grasped.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: First answer to the challenge of step 21.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A general rule of reasoning: pick the smaller, certain amount
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Maybe the gift should be fifty, like ערכין.
steps.terutzMaskana: When unsure between two sources, we take the smaller amount, thirty.
steps.whyThisMatters: 'תפשת מרובה לא תפשת' is a general rule used in many places across ש״ס whenever there is doubt between a larger and a smaller amount.

steps.title: Second answer: learn a slave law from a slave law
steps.stepSummary: Besides that, it makes more sense to learn the rule of a slave from another case about a slave.
steps.simpleTranslation: And furthermore, he should learn slave from slave.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a second answer. הענקה is about a slave, so the closest match is the gored slave, not ערכין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ערכין applies to all people. The ox case is specifically about a slave, just like הענקה. A comparison between two similar topics is stronger, so the thirty wins.

keyTerms.meaning: Slave from slave: learning a slave case from another slave case

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יהודה's thirty comes from the gored slave, not from ערכין' fifty, for two reasons: we take the smaller, certain amount, and we learn a slave case from a slave case.

phrases.aramaic: וְעוֹד, עֶבֶד מֵעֶבֶד הֲוָה לֵיהּ לְמֵילַף.
phrases.english: And furthermore, he should derive slave from slave.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְעוֹד, עֶבֶד מֵעֶבֶד הֲוָה לֵיהּ לְמֵילַף
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second answer to the challenge of step 21.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The source that matches the topic more closely wins
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Maybe ערכין is an equally good source.
steps.terutzMaskana: The gored slave is the better match because both cases are about a slave.

steps.title: רבי שמעון says the gift is fifty
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון rules that the הענקה is fifty shekels, like the fifty of ערכין.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון says: fifty, like the fifty of valuations.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues quoting the ברייתא and brings the third opinion, רבי שמעון, who says the master gives fifty shekels.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר said fifteen and רבי יהודה said thirty. רבי שמעון gives the biggest number, fifty, and ties it to the set value of a grown man in ערכין.

keyTerms.meaning: Valuations: set amounts a person pledges to the Temple based on someone's age and gender

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon says:
Fifty, like the fifty of valuations.
phrases.notes: In ערכין, a grown man's set value is fifty shekels (ויקרא 27:3).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Third opinion in the ברייתא, after רבי יהודה's thirty
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The הענקה is fifty shekels, like the ערך of a grown man.

steps.title: What is רבי שמעון's reason?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the source of רבי שמעון's fifty.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason of רבי שמעון?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks where רבי שמעון gets the number fifty. This sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just as the גמרא asked for רבי יהודה's source, it now asks the same about רבי שמעון. It is not attacking him, just looking for his source.

phrases.english: What is the reason of Rabbi Shimon?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the ruling just quoted

steps.title: He learns 'giving' from ערכין
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון links the word 'giving' in הענקה to the word 'giving' in ערכין, where the amount is fifty.
steps.simpleTranslation: He learns 'giving' and 'giving' from valuations: just as there it is fifty, so too here it is fifty.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers: רבי שמעון uses a גזירה שוה, matching the word 'giving' here with 'giving' in ערכין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה matched 'giving' with the slave gored by an ox (thirty). רבי שמעון uses the same word but matches it with ערכין, which gives fifty.

keyTerms.meaning: Giving: the shared word that makes the link
Just as there... so too here

phrases.english: He learns "giving" "giving" from valuations,
phrases.notes: In ערכין it says "ונתן" (ויקרא 27:23), and here it says "תתן לו" (דברים 15:14).

phrases.english: just as there it is fifty,
so too here it is fifty.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 25
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A גזירה שוה of 'giving' from ערכין, where the amount is fifty

steps.title: Why not the smallest amount in ערכין?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: ערכין has many amounts, so why not learn the smallest one?
steps.simpleTranslation: But say: like the smallest of the valuations!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back: if we learn from ערכין, why pick fifty and not the lowest amount there?
steps.deeperAnalysis: ערכין has a list of amounts, from fifty down to very small sums. The challenge is that the link to ערכין does not tell us which amount to use, so the smallest seems just as likely.

phrases.english: But say: like the smallest of the valuations!
phrases.notes: The smallest set value in ערכין is three shekels, for a baby girl (ויקרא 27:6).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the choice of fifty within ערכין
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי שמעון's choice of fifty out of all the ערכין amounts
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The link is to ערכין as a whole, so nothing forces the biggest amount over the smallest.

steps.title: The gift must be generous
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק says 'with which ה׳ your God has blessed you,' which calls for a generous amount.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is written: "With which ה׳ your God has blessed you."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the פסוק itself shows the gift must be generous, so we use the big amount, not the small one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'that ה׳ blessed you' tell us the master gives from his blessing, which means a respectable gift. That rules out the tiny ערך and points to fifty.

keyTerms.meaning: With which ה׳ your God has blessed you

phrases.english: "With which ה׳ your God has blessed you" is written.
phrases.notes: דברים 15:14

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 27
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We might use the smallest ערך
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Blessed you' requires a generous gift, so it is fifty

steps.title: Why not learn thirty from the slave, like רבי יהודה?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבי שמעון does not learn from the gored slave, which has two strong reasons in its favor.
steps.simpleTranslation: But let him learn 'giving' 'giving' from a slave: just as there it is thirty, so too here it is thirty. One, if you grabbed a lot you grabbed nothing; and also, he should learn slave from slave!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי שמעון: why not use רבי יהודה's link to the slave gored by an ox, which gives thirty?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא brings back the two reasons from before (steps 22-23): a smaller amount is safer, and a slave case should be learned from a slave case. Both seem to beat רבי שמעון's link to ערכין.

keyTerms.meaning: If you grab too much, you grab nothing
A slave from a slave: learning a case from a similar case

phrases.english: But let him learn "giving" "giving" from a slave,

phrases.aramaic: מָה לְהַלָּן שְׁלֹשִׁים – אַף כָּאן שְׁלֹשִׁים;
phrases.english: just as there it is thirty, so too here it is thirty;
one, that if you grabbed a lot, you did not grab,
phrases.notes: This is short for the saying from before: grab too much and you hold nothing; grab a little and you keep it.

phrases.aramaic: וְעוֹד, עֶבֶד מֵעֶבֶד הֲוָה לֵיהּ לְמֵילַף!
phrases.english: and furthermore, he should have learned slave from slave!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: New challenge to רבי שמעון's source, using רבי יהודה's reasoning
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי שמעון's choice of ערכין over the gored slave
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The slave link wins on two counts: the smaller amount is safer, and slave matches slave.

steps.title: רבי שמעון has a link based on 'becoming poor'
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון learns from the word 'poor,' which appears both in ערכין and by the עבד עברי.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון learns 'becoming poor' 'becoming poor.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבי שמעון's link to ערכין comes from a different word: 'becoming poor' shows up in both places.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רש״י explains that רבי שמעון's גזירה שווה was never from 'giving' at all. It comes from 'becoming poor,' a word written only by the עבד עברי and by ערכין. So he learns from ערכין, and the gored slave was never an option for him.

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon learns "becoming poor" "becoming poor."
phrases.notes: In ערכין: "ואם מך הוא" (ויקרא 27:8). By the עבד עברי: "וכי ימוך אחיך" (ויקרא 25:39).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 29
steps.terutzResolutionType: A second גזירה שוה that strengthens the link to ערכין
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי שמעון should learn thirty from the gored slave
steps.terutzMaskana: The word 'poor' connects the עבד עברי to ערכין, so he learns fifty
steps.whatToRemember: All three opinions: רבי מאיר says fifteen (five from ריקם by the בכור, applied to each of צאן, גורן, יקב), רבי יהודה says thirty (from the gored slave), רבי שמעון says fifty (from ערכין, backed by the word 'poor').

steps.title: Why do רבי יהודה and רבי שמעון need 'flock, threshing floor, and winepress'?
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר used these three words for his number; the other two need them for something else.
steps.simpleTranslation: It works for רבי מאיר: that is why it says flock, threshing floor, and winepress. But for רבי יהודה and רבי שמעון, why do I need this flock, threshing floor, and winepress?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks: if רבי יהודה and רבי שמעון get their numbers from other places, what do the words 'flock, threshing floor, and winepress' teach them?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every word in the תורה should teach something. רבי מאיר used these words for his amount, but the other two did not, so the words seem to have no job in their view.

keyTerms.meaning: It works well (for one view, but not the other)

phrases.english: It works well for Rabbi Meir,
that is why it is written flock, threshing floor, and winepress.
phrases.notes: רבי מאיר learned his amount of fifteen from these three words.

phrases.english: but according to Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon,

phrases.aramaic: הַאי צֹאן גּוֹרֶן וָיֶקֶב לְמָה לִי?
phrases.english: why do I need this flock, threshing floor, and winepress?

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּשְׁלָמָא לְרַבִּי מֵאִיר הַיְינוּ דִּכְתִיב צֹאן גּוֹרֶן וָיֶקֶב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After all sources are set, the גמרא looks at words that seem unused
steps.kashyaTarget: The views of רבי יהודה and רבי שמעון
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The words צאן, גורן, יקב seem to teach nothing in their view.

steps.title: The words teach that the gift must be something that grows
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא shows these words teach that the gift must be something 'blessed' that grows, which leaves out money.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is needed for what was taught: one might think the gift comes only from flock, threshing floor, and winepress. How do we include everything? The verse says 'with which ה׳ blessed you.' If so, why mention flock, threshing floor, and winepress? To teach that just as these are special in being part of blessing, so too anything that is part of blessing; money is left out. These are the words of רבי שמעון.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a ברייתא: the three words are examples that teach what kind of thing may be given, namely things that grow and multiply.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'that ה׳ blessed you' widen the gift to all kinds of items. The three examples then narrow it to things like them, things that grow. Money does not grow by itself, so according to רבי שמעון it is not used for the gift.

keyTerms.meaning: As was taught in a ברייתא
Part of blessing: things that grow and multiply

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix this up with the amount. These words are not about how much to give; they tell us what kind of thing may be given.

phrases.english: This is needed for what was taught in a ברייתא:
One might think that they give the parting gift
only from flock, threshing floor, and winepress;
from where do we include every item?
The verse says: "with which ה׳ your God has blessed you."

phrases.aramaic: אִם כֵּן מָה תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר צֹאן גּוֹרֶן וָיֶקֶב?
phrases.english: If so, why does the verse say flock, threshing floor, and winepress?
To tell you:
just as flock, threshing floor, and winepress are special
in that they are part of blessing,
so too anything that is part of blessing;
money is left out,
these are the words of Rabbi Shimon.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 31 by giving the words a different job
steps.terutzResolutionType: The words are needed for a different teaching
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The words צאן, גורן, יקב have no use for רבי יהודה and רבי שמעון
steps.terutzMaskana: They define the type of gift: things that grow, which leaves out money
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows the הענקה is meant to be something that can keep growing for the freed slave, not just a sum of cash.

steps.title: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב: mules are left out
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב says the rule of 'blessing' leaves out mules.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב says: mules are left out.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא brings a second view on what the 'blessing' rule leaves out: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב says mules.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both agree the gift must be something that is 'blessed.' They differ on what fails that test: רבי שמעון says money, while רבי אליעזר בן יעקב says mules.
steps.whatToRemember: The words צאן, גורן, יקב teach that the gift must be something 'blessed.' רבי שמעון says this leaves out money; רבי אליעזר בן יעקב says it leaves out mules.

phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says:
mules are left out.
phrases.notes: Mules can't have babies, so they don't grow and multiply like a 'blessing.'

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב אוֹמֵר יָצְאוּ פְּרָדוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second view within the ברייתא on what the 'blessing' rule leaves out
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Mules may not be given as the הענקה because they do not reproduce.

steps.title: Why רבי שמעון does not leave out mules
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבי שמעון does not also leave out mules. It answers that mules' bodies grow bigger and better, so they count as 'blessed.'
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי שמעון, why does he not leave out mules? Because mules grow and improve in their bodies.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רבי שמעון does not agree with רבי אליעזר בן יעקב and leave out mules, and then answers its own question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אליעזר בן יעקב said mules are not 'blessed' because they cannot have babies. רבי שמעון says growth does not have to mean having babies. A mule's own body gets bigger and more valuable, and that is enough to count as 'blessed.'

keyTerms.meaning: Mules, animals that cannot have offspring
They improve and increase in value

phrases.english: And Rabbi Shimon, why doesn't he leave out mules?
Mules grow and improve in their bodies.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why רבי שמעון does not accept רבי אליעזר בן יעקב's exclusion of mules from Step 33.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why רבי שמעון does not exclude mules from the הענקה.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Mules grow physically and increase in value, so they count as 'blessed.'

steps.title: Why רבי אליעזר בן יעקב does not leave out money
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבי אליעזר בן יעקב does not leave out money. It answers that a person can do business with money and make it grow.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי אליעזר בן יעקב, why does he not leave out money? Because a person can do business with money.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רבי אליעזר בן יעקב does not agree with רבי שמעון and leave out money, and then answers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי שמעון said money is not 'blessed' because it does not grow by itself. רבי אליעזר בן יעקב says money can grow through business, so it counts as 'blessed.' Each opinion has a different idea of what 'growing' means.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי שמעון leaves out money but includes mules, because mules grow in their bodies. רבי אליעזר בן יעקב leaves out mules but includes money, because money can grow through business.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, why doesn't he leave out money?
With money, one can do business.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Mirrors Step 34: explains the other side of the disagreement.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why רבי אליעזר בן יעקב does not exclude money from the הענקה.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Money can grow through business, so it counts as 'blessed.'

steps.title: Why the תורה needed both 'flock' and 'threshing floor'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that both words are needed. From 'flock' alone we would include only animals. From 'threshing floor' alone we would include only things that grow from the ground.
steps.simpleTranslation: Both are needed. If the תורה wrote only 'flock,' I would think animals are included but things that grow from the ground are not, so the תורה wrote 'threshing floor.' If it wrote only 'threshing floor,' I would think things from the ground are included but animals are not, so the תורה wrote 'flock.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows that each word in the פסוק teaches something the other word could not teach alone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Animals and crops are two different kinds of 'blessed' things. One example would not tell us about the other kind. So the תורה needed one example of each.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed (both parts are necessary)
Things that grow from the ground

phrases.english: And it is needed, because if the Merciful One had written only 'flock,'
phrases.notes: The פסוק is דברים 15:14, which lists 'your flock, your threshing floor, and your winepress.'

phrases.english: I would have said: animals, yes,
things that grow from the ground, no;
so the Merciful One wrote 'threshing floor.'
And if He had written only 'threshing floor,'
I would have said: things that grow from the ground, yes,
animals, no;
so the Merciful One wrote 'flock.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After finishing the disagreement, the גמרא turns to why the פסוק lists more than one example.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Both 'flock' and 'threshing floor' are needed: one teaches animals, the other teaches things that grow from the ground.

steps.title: Why is 'winepress' needed?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: since 'threshing floor' already teaches things that grow from the ground, why does the תורה also write 'winepress'?
steps.simpleTranslation: Why do I need 'winepress'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why the third word, 'winepress,' is in the פסוק, and sets up the answer that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wine comes from grapes, which also grow from the ground. 'Threshing floor' already covers that kind of thing. So 'winepress' seems extra, and the גמרא wants to know what it adds.
